- *Flat*: every heading with at least one recognized contact property (~:EMAIL:~, ~:PHONE:~, ~:CELL:~, ~:WORK_PHONE:~, ~:ADDRESS:~, ~:ADR:~, ~:NICKNAME:~, ~:NOTE:~, ~:ANNIVERSARY:~ or the birthday property). ~:IGNORE: t~ excludes one. A heading with none is skipped.
- *Tree*: a contact heading (~:KIND: individual~, ~:FIELDTYPE: name~) with each field as a descendant heading carrying its own ~:FIELDTYPE:~, at any depth. A contact with no fields still exports a minimal vCard (~FN~, ~N~).

The *To: new buffer* checkbox sends the vCard text to a new unsaved document (a ~vCard(s)~ heading, titled ~*scratch*~) instead of downloading a file; Import reads that shape back.

There are no name, tag or property filters. *This file* respects an active narrow restriction ([[#narrowing][subtree narrowing]] or [[#searching][Search's Narrow]]), and the screen says so; narrow first, then export. A narrow applies only to the open document, never to Contacts Files.

| Org source (flat) | vCard field | Notes |
|---+---+---|
| Heading title | ~FN~ | |
| ~:N:~ | ~N~ | Used as given; if absent, split from the title (last word as family name) |
| ~:EMAIL:~ | ~EMAIL~ | |
| ~:EMAIL_LABEL:~ | ~LABEL="..."~ on the ~EMAIL~ line | When present |
| ~:PHONE:~, ~:CELL:~ | ~TEL~ | |
| ~:PHONE_LABEL:~ | ~LABEL="..."~ on the ~TEL~ line | |
| ~:WORK_PHONE:~ | ~TEL;TYPE=WORK~ | |
| ~:ADDRESS:~, ~:ADR:~ | ~ADR~ | Placed in the street component, since an address is one free-text string here |
| ~:ADDRESS_LABEL:~ | ~LABEL="..."~ on the ~ADR~ line | |
| ~:ADDRESS_RAW:~ | The structured ~;;street;city;region;postal;country~ part of ~ADR~ | The seven components, kept verbatim and used when present |
| ~:NICKNAME:~ | ~NICKNAME~ | |
| ~:ORG:~ | ~ORG~ | Several ~;~-separated parts are joined into one string |
| ~:JOB_TITLE:~ | ~TITLE~ | |
| ~:URL:~ | ~URL~ | |
| ~:URL_LABEL:~ | ~LABEL="..."~ on the ~URL~ line | |
| ~:PHOTO:~ | ~PHOTO~ | An ~http~ or ~https~ URL as is; an embedded photo as a ~data:~ URI (to display photos, see [[#local-variables][~org-xx-startup-with-show-photos~]]) |
| ~:NOTE:~ | ~NOTE~ | |
| A heading's tags | ~CATEGORIES~ | ~:CATEGORIES_RAW:~ is preferred when present |
| ~:CATEGORIES_RAW:~ | ~CATEGORIES~ | The original comma-separated text; tags can't hold spaces, so "Other Account" would otherwise become ~Other_Account~ |
| ~org-contacts-birthday-property~ (default ~BIRTHDAY~) | ~BDAY~ | Accepts a bare ~YYYY-MM-DD~ with no description |
| ~:ANNIVERSARY:~ | ~ANNIVERSARY~ (~YYYYMMDD~) | A vCard 4.0 property, written in the 3.0 card as a phone's own export does |
| ~:SPOUSE:~ | ~RELATED;TYPE=spouse;VALUE=text~ | Likewise |

| Tree style ~:FIELDTYPE:~ | vCard field | Notes |
|---+---+---|
| ~name~ | The contact itself | Needs ~:KIND: individual~ on the same heading |
| ~n~ | ~N~ | Used as given; else split from the title |
| ~cell~ | ~TEL;TYPE=CELL~ | A ~:LABEL:~ property becomes a ~LABEL="..."~ parameter, here and in the rows below |
| ~phone~, ~phone-work~, ~phone-home~ | ~TEL~, ~TEL;TYPE=WORK~, ~TEL;TYPE=HOME~ | |
| ~email~, ~email-work~, ~email-home~ | ~EMAIL~, ~EMAIL;TYPE=WORK~, ~EMAIL;TYPE=HOME~ | |
| ~address~ | ~ADR~ | Street component. A ~:RAW:~ property holds the seven preserved components, and a ~#+BEGIN_VERSE~ or ~#+BEGIN_QUOTE~ block in the body becomes the ~LABEL~ |
| ~address-work~, ~address-home~ | ~ADR;TYPE=WORK~, ~ADR;TYPE=HOME~ | |
| ~nickname~ | ~NICKNAME~ | |
| ~org~ | ~ORG~ | |
| ~job-title~ | ~TITLE~ | |
| ~url~ | ~URL~ | |
| ~photo~ | ~PHOTO~ | A URL is the heading's title. An embedded photo is titled "Photo", with its ~data:~ URI in a ~:DATA:~ property |
| ~note~ | ~NOTE~ | Read from a ~#+BEGIN_VERSE~ or ~#+BEGIN_QUOTE~ block in the body, not the title |
| ~birthday~ | ~BDAY~ | A bare ~YYYY-MM-DD~ is accepted |
| ~anniversary~ | ~ANNIVERSARY~ | |
| ~spouse~ | ~RELATED;TYPE=spouse~ | |
| A contact's tags | ~CATEGORIES~ | ~:CATEGORIES_RAW:~ on the contact heading is preferred |

Both styles cover the same set of fields, which is smaller than org-vcard's full mapping. ~:PREFERRED:~ is accepted but doesn't yet affect field order or add a ~PREF~ parameter.

*** What is dropped

Property drawers and ~ARCHIVE_*~ properties (see [[#archiving][Archiving]]) are not exported. SCHEDULED and DEADLINE show as a small italic line under the heading in Markdown, HTML and ODT; Calendar is built from them.

** Import
:PROPERTIES:
:CUSTOM_ID: import
:END:

*More → Import* lists the formats it reads, as Export does: *Contacts (.vcf)* and *iCalendar (.ics)*. Each opens its own panel. The palette commands are ~org-vcard-import~ and ~icalendar-import-file~.

*Contacts (.vcf)* is the reverse of [[#export][Contacts (.vcf) export]]. A ~.vcf~ file can hold one contact or many, and each becomes a new heading appended to the end of the open document. Nothing already in the file is touched.

*Style*: *Flat* or *Tree*, the two structures Export supports, independent of the style you last exported. Tree is the default, because Flat keeps only one value per field type (see below). Exporting a contact, importing that file and exporting again gives an equivalent vCard.

*Sources*: *Choose vCard file…*, *Choose a heading…* and *This file*. A document can hold headings whose body is vCard text, such as Export's *To: new buffer* output or text you paste in. *Choose a heading…* scans that heading and its descendants for bodies starting with ~BEGIN:VCARD~, and *This file* scans the whole document. Both say plainly when there is nothing to import ("No vCard data found in this file"). The *To: new buffer* checkbox sends the imported contacts to a new unsaved ~*scratch*~ document instead of appending to the open one.

*What is read*: ~FN~ is the only required property, as in [[https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6350][RFC 6350]]; a vCard block without one is skipped. ~N~, ~EMAIL~, ~TEL~, ~ADR~, ~URL~, ~NICKNAME~, ~ORG~, ~TITLE~, ~PHOTO~, ~NOTE~, ~BDAY~ and ~CATEGORIES~ are mapped when present, the reverse of Export's tables.

- ~N~ is kept exactly as given, never recomputed from ~FN~ (which would mangle a business name or a single name).
- ~ADR~'s components (PO Box, street, city, region, postal code, country) are joined into one comma-separated string.
- A value with embedded newlines (a multi-line ~NOTE~ or ~ADR~) becomes one line, with a space-semicolon-space separator, wherever it lands in a single-line Flat property.
- ~CATEGORIES~ become org tags on the heading, and export writes them back as ~CATEGORIES:~.
- Folded (continued) lines are unfolded, and escapes (~\,~, ~\;~, ~\\~, ~\n~) are reversed, the inverse of Export's escaping.

*Apple and Google ~itemN.~ grouping*: these contacts tie a label to a property with a group prefix, such as ~item1.TEL~ with ~item1.X-ABLabel~ (standard vCard 3.0). This is always recognized, because otherwise the prefixed properties would be dropped. The label becomes ~:EMAIL_LABEL:~, ~:PHONE_LABEL:~ or ~:URL_LABEL:~ (Flat), or a ~:LABEL:~ property on the field heading (Tree), like ~:ADDRESS_LABEL:~ for addresses. A label you assigned ("Landline") is kept as is. Apple's placeholder form (~"_$!<HomePage>!$_"~) is reduced to its inner name ("HomePage"), and an empty label or Apple's "no label" placeholder (~"_$!!$_"~) gives no label. ~URL~ can have several values. Apple's ~X-ABADR~ country-code companion is ignored.

*Clean data (Google, Apple)* is a checkbox, on by default, for non-standard quirks of those exports:

1. Google appends an eighth component to ~ADR~: the address again, as a multi-line label. On, it is kept alongside the seven structured components, so a later export can rebuild the original. Off, it is ignored, as RFC 6350's seven-component ~ADR~ requires. The standard ~ADR;LABEL="..."~ parameter is recognized either way.
2. Google escapes colons as ~\:~, which isn't a real vCard escape. On, it is turned back into ~:~ everywhere; off, it is left as written.
3. Apple's ~X-ABLabel~ placeholders are interpreted as described above; off, they are stored as written.

*Flat style keeps one value per type*: one ~:EMAIL:~, ~:PHONE:~ or ~:WORK_PHONE:~, ~:URL:~ and ~:ADDRESS:~. When a vCard has several of one type, the first is kept and the rest are dropped, so use Tree style to keep them all (org-vcard lists multiple ~EMAIL~ as an open item too). Labels survive as ~:ADDRESS_LABEL:~, ~:EMAIL_LABEL:~, ~:PHONE_LABEL:~ and ~:URL_LABEL:~.

*Tree style has no such limit*: each value becomes its own descendant heading. The ~address-work~ and ~address-home~ fieldtypes (like ~email-work~ and ~phone-home~ in Export's table) round-trip a ~TYPE=WORK~ or ~TYPE=HOME~ address. A field whose value contains a newline (a note, always, or a Google address whose label spans lines) gets a fixed title ("Note", "Home Address") with its text as a ~#+BEGIN_VERSE~ block in the body. Verse keeps every line break, so separate facts (old phone numbers, street and city) don't blur together, and a body can hold newlines that Flat must flatten. Export reads ~#+BEGIN_VERSE~ or ~#+BEGIN_QUOTE~ and falls back to the heading's title when there is neither. A short single-line label is a plain ~:LABEL:~ property on the field heading.

*Warnings*: properties the parser doesn't know are collected, listed once by name in the status message after the import ("Imported 3 contacts from vCard. 2 unrecognized properties were skipped: X-SOCIALPROFILE, X-YAHOO."). ~VERSION~, ~PRODID~, ~REV~, ~UID~ and ~X-ABADR~ are known and deliberately unmapped, so they aren't reported. A base64 ~PHOTO~ gets its own count in the same message, since it is kept as a ~data:~ URI (see Export's ~:PHOTO:~ row).

~ANNIVERSARY~ and a ~RELATED;TYPE=spouse~ name become ~:ANNIVERSARY:~ and ~:SPOUSE:~; other relations are reported as skipped. A ~.vcf~ file with no valid (~FN~) contacts gives a clear status message. A malformed line inside an otherwise valid contact is skipped without aborting the import.

*iCalendar (.ics)* is the reverse of [[#export][Calendar (.ics) export]], and reads a calendar exported from Google, Apple, Outlook or Nextcloud. Each event becomes a new heading appended to the end of the open document, and each task a TODO heading. Nothing already in the file is touched. The sources are the same as for Contacts: *Choose iCalendar file…*, *Choose a heading…* and *This file* (which look for bodies starting with ~BEGIN:VCALENDAR~), and the *To: new buffer* checkbox, which has its own setting. There is no style or clean-up option.

- An event's time is a timestamp in the heading's title, where the agenda looks for one: ~* Dentist <2026-10-05 Mon 09:00-10:30>~. An all-day event has a date only. A multi-day event is a range, ~<2026-10-05 Mon>--<2026-10-07 Wed>~, which the agenda shows on its first and last day.
- Times are shown in this device's time zone. A time in UTC or in a named zone (~TZID~) is converted, as Emacs's ~icalendar-import-file~ does. A time with no zone is kept as written, and so is one in a zone name the browser doesn't know (Outlook's own names, for example); the status line says so.
- ~LOCATION~, ~URL~ and ~UID~ become properties, ~CATEGORIES~ become tags, ~DESCRIPTION~ becomes the body, and a cancelled event keeps ~:STATUS: CANCELLED~.
- A recurrence becomes a repeater when one says the same thing (~FREQ~ with ~INTERVAL~, such as ~+1w~). A rule a repeater cannot express (an end date or ~COUNT~, several weekdays, "the second Tuesday") is imported once, at its first date, with the rule in an ~:RRULE:~ property, and the status line counts them. Nothing becomes a repeater that would run on the wrong days or for ever.
- A task (~VTODO~) becomes a ~TODO~ heading, or ~DONE~ with ~CLOSED~ once completed. ~DUE~ is its ~DEADLINE~, ~DTSTART~ its ~SCHEDULED~, and ~PRIORITY~ becomes ~[#A]~, ~[#B]~ or ~[#C]~.
- Attendees, organizer, attachments and exceptions (~EXDATE~) are not carried over, and the status line names them ("Imported 2 events and 1 task from iCalendar. 1 unrecognized property was skipped: ATTENDEE."). Alarms are ignored.

** Help
:PROPERTIES:
:CUSTOM_ID: docs
:END:

Open Help from the palette's *Help* (or god-mode's ~h SPC m~). It is this file, ~README.org~, opened read-only in its own last tab; opening it again switches to it. It opens with ~#+STARTUP: show2levels~.

-----

** Settings
:PROPERTIES:
:CUSTOM_ID: settings
:END:

Reached via *More (⋮) → Settings*, which replaces the outline until you navigate away, like switching views. Settings opens on a list of six categories, each a page of small cards: *Appearance*, *Editing and startup*, *Agenda and weather*, *Sync and storage*, *Export* and *Advanced*. At the foot of the list, *Check for updates* is centred on a line of its own, with the version centred beneath it; the result of the check (or “Out of date — reload”) appears on that line in bold red. Tap one to open it and *‹ Settings* to come back; a number on a category counts what you have set there: changed Quick Settings, connected services, ticked export items. *Search settings* finds a card from any category. In a window wide enough (about 720 px), the categories become a sidebar with the page beside it. Settings reopens on the page you left.

*Order of settings* (Advanced) moves categories, and the cards inside each, up or down with ▲ ▼; *Reset to default order* puts them back. The order is kept on the device and travels with *Export Settings*.

The cards, by what they hold:

- *Quick Settings*: labeled controls for the Global and Local Variables the app supports (see [[#local-variables][Local Variables]]), grouped by area, with an *Advanced* group for those with more complex syntax (refile targets, agenda files, the ~org-xx-*~ menu variables; see [[#extras-menu][Extras menu]] and [[#menu-customization][Menu customization]]). It shares storage with the Global Variables text box, so each reflects changes made in the other.
- *Global Variables* and *Capture Templates*: raw ~name: value~ lines and raw JSON, each edited in a popup.
- *GitHub* and *WebDAV*: connection details for each backend. Use a fine-grained GitHub token scoped to just that repository (Contents read and write only), and for WebDAV an app-specific password if your server offers one.
- *Calendar (CalDAV) / Contacts (CardDAV)*: the calendar your agenda is mirrored to and the address book your contacts are, right after WebDAV (see [[#calendar-sync][Calendar and contacts sync]]).
- *Agenda notifications*: reminders before appointments, just before GitHub (see [[#agenda-notifications][Agenda notifications]]).
- *Appearance*: theme (System, Light or Dark), fonts, independent font sizes for main text, tables and menus, reading width, custom colors for Light and Dark, and *Paragraph Spacing*. Paragraph Spacing is two independent values laid out like the font sizes: one for paragraphs and one, *Tables*, for tables and other secondary blocks (source and quote blocks, rules). Each is 0 to 32px with a 10px default. Where a paragraph meets a table or block the larger value applies, and headings and list items space themselves.
- *Backup*: *Export Settings* saves everything on this page as JSON; *Import Settings* merges a file back in, leaving other settings untouched.
- *Updates*: shows the running version and checks for a new one. If a newer version is installed but this page predates it, a banner offers *Reload*. The Android app has no button.
- *Export* (General, ASCII, HTML, LaTeX): one card per export type. *General* sets a *Page header* and *Page footer* for printed pages (~Draft | | %d~ is left, centre, right). *HTML* sets a *Preamble*, *Postamble* and *Head*, with an option to add a table of contents with page numbers when printing. *LaTeX* sets the class and compiler, with an option that fixes wide TOC numbers. Each has a tick box and is off until ticked; a ticked item applies to every export whose file doesn't set its own. A *Format codes* list explains ~%t~, ~%a~, ~%d~, ~%p~, ~%P~ and the rest.

A file's own ~#+STARTUP:~ or Local Variables block still overrides an app-wide default set here.

-----

** Offline behavior and sync
:PROPERTIES:
:CUSTOM_ID: offline-behavior-and-sync
:END:

Edits are cached locally at once; writing to disk, GitHub or WebDAV happens only on an explicit Save.

*Conflict detection*: Save compares the file's current state with what the app last knew, so one version never silently overwrites the other. The app also checks for external changes when a file is opened, when the tab regains focus, and when you switch into a tab with real backing storage. A banner then appears with *Merge*, *Reload* and *Dismiss*. For a local file this background check never asks the browser for permission: it runs only if access is already granted, so the banner may not appear until you have saved or reloaded the file in the session. Save, Reload and Merge still ask when they need to.

*Resolving a conflict*: the app keeps the full text of the file as of the last successful open or save, the common ancestor a three-way merge needs. When Save finds the file changed elsewhere under your unsaved edits, it compares the ancestor, your version and the other one line by line:

- *The other version has no real change, or matches yours*: Save just proceeds. A server that changes a file's ETag without changing its content isn't a conflict.
- *Your changes and theirs are in different places*: they are combined automatically and Save completes with a status message (~Saved — merged with the changes made elsewhere~). The merge is its own undo step (*Merged with changes from elsewhere*), so Undo returns to your text from just before it.
- *Both sides changed the same lines*, or adjacent lines with no unchanged line between them (the same place, as in git and GNU diff3): a dialog lists each such region with your version and the other one. Choose *Yours*, *Other* or *Both* (yours, then theirs) for each, or *All yours* or *All other* for every region at once. *Apply* stays disabled until every region has a decision, and everything outside the regions is already combined. *Cancel*, Escape or tapping outside changes nothing: the other version is untouched, your edits stay unsaved, and the next Save raises the same conflict.
- *No common ancestor is known* (a file last synced by a version that didn't keep one, until its next open or save), or the two versions are too different to compare by lines: every difference, or the whole file as one choice, is shown for you to decide.

*The banner's Merge* does the same without waiting for Save. It combines your unsaved edits with the version now stored, asks about clashing regions in the same dialog, and applies the result as an ordinary, undoable, still-unsaved edit. The other version becomes the new baseline, so the Save that follows is a plain write. With no unsaved changes Merge just reloads, and a read-only buffer can't be merged into (make it writable first).

*What this isn't*: the merge works on lines, not org structure. A subtree moved on one side and edited on the other is an ordinary clash, and two sides that each add the same new heading in different places keep both. A clean automatic merge is still worth a glance; that is what the undo step is for.

-----

** Platform support
:PROPERTIES:
:CUSTOM_ID: platform-support
:END:

Local file access ("Local", a live writable handle) requires the File System Access API -- Chrome/Edge, desktop or Android. Not supported on iOS, a WebKit limitation.

On unsupported platforms, *Import* replaces "Local": pick a file, edit it, and Save downloads the new version for you to move into place yourself. GitHub and WebDAV work the same everywhere, including iOS.

*Sharing into the app*: Android's Share sheet and the icon's *Capture* shortcut work for the installed app. iOS has no equivalent, so use the clipboard (~%x~); see [[#capture-from-other-apps][Capturing from other apps]].

*** Android app
:PROPERTIES:
:CUSTOM_ID: android-app
:END:

The Android app is the same app in a native wrapper, with a few things done the Android way.

- *Local files*: *File → Open → Local file* uses Android's file picker, and the app keeps access to the file, so Save writes straight back and the file reopens from the recent list. *Save As → Local file* names a new one. The picker starts in ~Documents/org-pwa~, in the shared Documents folder where a file manager finds it, and you can choose any other folder. A file is known by its name, so two files with the same name from different folders replace each other.
- *Agenda files*: ~local:name.org~ names a file in the org-pwa folder (below), like ~github:journal.org;local:home.org~. It loads silently and read-only; a file you opened with *Open → Local file* works too, and so does one added with the command *Add a local file* (command palette), which remembers the file without opening it.
- *Attaching a file*: *Attach* opens Android's chooser with the camera apps beside your files, as the browser's does. Pick *Take a photo* or *Record a video*, and the result is attached.
- *Saving a file out*: exports and settings backups go straight into the *Downloads* folder, and the status line says so.
- *The org-pwa folder*: the first time something needs it (a local file's first attachment, or a ~local:~ name that isn't found), the app asks you to choose a folder, starting at ~Documents/org-pwa~. Attachments go under ~data/~ inside it, as on GitHub and WebDAV, and ~local:~ files are found in it by name, anywhere a ~github:~ or ~webdav:~ file can be named: ~org-agenda-files~, ~org-contacts-files~, ~org-refile-targets~, a capture template's ~file~, a link or ~#+INCLUDE~. ~local:contacts.org~ is ~contacts.org~ in that folder, and ~local:areas/home.org~ is ~home.org~ in its ~areas~ folder. A file you opened with the file picker is found by its name first. *Choose the org-pwa folder* changes it.
- *Reminders*: agenda notifications (see [[#agenda-notifications][Agenda notifications]]) are handed to Android, so they arrive with the app closed. Allow notifications when asked; without the *Alarms & reminders* setting they may be a few minutes late.
- *Long-press the app icon*: your capture templates are listed, in the order they are in *Settings → Capture Templates*, as many as the launcher shows. Tapping one opens that template. Drag one onto the home screen for an icon, or run *Add a capture icon to the home screen*.
- *Sharing in*: share a link or text from any app to *org-pwa*; Capture opens with it (see [[#capture-from-other-apps][Capturing from other apps]]).
- *Separate from the browser*: the app keeps its own settings, tokens and documents, so enter GitHub, WebDAV, calendar and contacts settings again. A WebDAV, CalDAV or CardDAV server must allow the origin ~https://localhost~ (CORS).
- *Updates*: the app is updated by installing a newer APK over the old one. *Settings → Updates* shows which version you have.

*Screen size*: mobile-first below 900px wide. Above that, Settings and Help open in a resizable side panel next to the outline instead of replacing it, and the app uses the full window width. Reading width is unlimited by default; Settings → Appearance has an opt-in narrower column.

No auto-capitalization anywhere in this app.

-----

** Command palette
:PROPERTIES:
:CUSTOM_ID: command-palette
:END:

A searchable list of what the app can do, the touch counterpart of Emacs's ~M-x~. Open it from *More → Commands* (first by default) or, from a keyboard, in [[#god-mode][god-mode]] with ~g x~ (which is ~M-x~) or ~h SPC a~ (~C-h a~).

*Searching*: type a few letters or words. Each word must match the command's name, the real Org or Emacs command it corresponds to, or one of a few extra keywords (so ~deadline~ finds *Edit details*). Case doesn't matter. Real names work as you'd type them in ~M-x~: ~org-clock-in~ finds *Clock in* but not *Clock out*, because a hyphenated word is matched as that exact phrase, while ~clock in~ typed with a space is two words that can match anywhere. A category name (*Clocking*, *Heading*, *Export*) also matches at the start of its words. There is no fuzzy or skip-letter matching.

*Order*: commands that can run now come first, then the rest, dimmed, each saying why it can't (*nothing is narrowed*, *no clock is running*, *the buffer is read-only*, *tap a heading first*). A command is never mysteriously absent, and choosing a dimmed one repeats the reason as a status message. With nothing typed, your most recently used commands come first (marked ~↺~), remembered across sessions. ↑ and ↓ move the highlight, Enter or a tap runs it, and Escape or a tap outside closes it.

*What it acts on*: heading commands work on the heading whose action menu is open (tap a heading's title first), else the keyboard-focused heading. A command that needs a heading and can't find one says so, except *Add heading after* and *Add TODO heading after*, which also work with nothing selected (see the table in [[#keybindings][Keybindings]] for where the new heading lands).

*Names*: a command's real Emacs or Org function name is shown beside it and is searchable. The same name, quoted, names the command in an Extras-menu entry (see [[#extras-menu][Extras menu]]), so the palette, the god-mode chords and Extras share one vocabulary. The commands with no real name are this app's own: *New document*, *Undo history*, *Sync agenda to calendar*, *Rebuild calendar from the agenda*, *Show display measurements*, *Add a capture icon to the home screen*, *Choose the org-pwa folder* and *Add a local file*. A command with a [[#god-mode][god-mode]] key runs the same code as that key and shows it.

*What's in it*, by group:

| Group | Commands |
|---+---|
| *Heading* | cycle TODO state, set priority, set effort estimate, edit details (schedule, deadline, timestamps, tags, properties), add heading or TODO heading after, promote, demote, move up, move down, cut, paste, archive, unarchive, refile, attachments, narrow, widen |
| *Clocking* | clock in, clock out, cancel clock, continue last clock, go to clocked task, go to a recently clocked task |
| *Document* | save, save as, open, new, undo, redo, undo history, toggle read-only, capture, recalculate all tables |
| *View* | agenda, TODO list, outline view, text view, cycle visibility of the whole document, calendar, search, sync agenda to calendar, rebuild calendar, sync contacts to the address book, rebuild contacts |
| *Export* | the Export menu; this file as HTML, LaTeX, Markdown or ASCII |
| *Import* | Contacts (.vcf), ~org-vcard-import~; iCalendar (.ics), ~icalendar-import-file~ |
| *App* | settings, help, show display measurements, add a capture icon to the home screen and choose the org-pwa folder (Android app only) |

*Also in it*: your own capture templates and [[#extras-menu][Extras menu]] entries, one command each. *Capture: <description>* (such as *Capture: Meeting*) runs that template directly, and *Extras: <label>* runs that Extras entry as tapping it would. Both are read fresh each time the palette opens, so an edited template list or a document's own Extras menu (set in its Local Variables) is current. The plain *Capture* command still opens the template picker.

*Commands*, like the other More entries, can be renamed, hidden or reordered with [[#menu-customization][menu customization]] (~org-xx-menu-aliases~). It is the ordinary ~more:~ label ~Commands~, which renders first by default.


** Security and privacy
:PROPERTIES:
:CUSTOM_ID: security-and-privacy
:END:

There is no server of ours: the app talks only to the places you set up, and nothing is sent anywhere else.

*Where things are kept.* Your files stay where they are (a file on the device, GitHub or WebDAV). The app keeps its settings in the browser's own storage on this device, including the GitHub token, the WebDAV, calendar and contacts passwords, and the init script. They are stored as plain text, as in any browser app, so use a token limited to one repository and an app-specific password, and sign out of a shared device by clearing its site data. Nothing but what you set up is synced, exported or read from a file.

*What can run.* Only the app's own code runs in the page. The page's Content-Security-Policy refuses inline and injected scripts. Code from a document or the init script runs in a [[#extensions][sandbox]] with no access to the page, your files or your tokens. It reaches a server only if you allow it.

** Keybindings
:PROPERTIES:
:CUSTOM_ID: keybindings
:END:

A practical subset for a keyboard or mouse. On a phone or tablet it applies only to a paired Bluetooth keyboard.

These are *not org's own bindings*, on purpose. Org leans on the ~C-c~ prefix, and ~C-c~, ~C-v~, ~C-a~ and ~C-f~ are reserved by browsers for copy, paste, select-all and find, so a page can't reliably take them; org's ~M-←~ and ~M-→~ collide with the browser's back and forward. Where org's key is safe it is used as is; otherwise a safe key stands in. god-mode (below) reaches org's fuller set.

| Key | Action | Matches real org? |
|---+---+---|
| ~↓~, ~↑~ | Move keyboard focus to the next or previous visible line: any row (heading, paragraph, table, list item, block). Moving down into a folded heading reveals its first body row. A status message reports the first or last line | No equivalent |
| ~S-↓~, ~S-↑~, ~S-←~, ~S-→~ | Only with focus on a table: move cell by cell (the header row counts; a rule between rows doesn't). Outside a table they aren't intercepted. After you edit a cell by tap, ~Enter~ commits and ~Escape~ cancels (the *⎌* button does the same by tap), and the cell stays highlighted for more Shift+arrow navigation. Clicking anything that isn't a table cell clears it | No equivalent |
| ~i~ | Edit the current line (heading title, paragraph, table cell or list item), cursor at the start | Like vim's ~i~ |
| ~j~, ~k~ | Move focus to the next or previous visible heading, faster than ~↓~ and ~↑~. A status message reports the first or last heading | Vim-style |
| ~Tab~ | Cycle the focused heading's fold state | Yes, ~org-cycle~ |
| ~Enter~ | Open or close the focused heading's action row | No equivalent |
| ~/~ | Focus the search box | A web convention |
| ~Escape~ | The first that applies: cancel a god-mode sequence, exit god-mode, clear keyboard focus, enter god-mode | A web convention, extended for god-mode |

Keyboard focus, a thin highlight around the focused row, is separate from tapping a heading open. It starts unset; the first arrow, ~j~ or ~k~ picks the first or last visible heading, and shortcuts that need the focused heading do nothing until one exists. ~Tab~ follows the same archived-heading rule as the swipe gesture (see [[#local-variables][Local Variables]]). Shortcuts never fire while you are typing in a text field, and Ctrl and Cmd combinations are never intercepted, so the browser's copy, paste and find stay safe.

Cycling TODO state, moving a heading, promoting and demoting, and inserting a heading are available by tap, in god-mode (~c t~, ~g↑~ and ~g↓~, ~g←~ and ~g→~, ~gRET~), and from the command palette (*Add heading after*).

*** god-mode
:PROPERTIES:
:CUSTOM_ID: god-mode
:END:

An alternate input mode that reaches org's fuller keybinding set (~C-c C-t~, ~M-RET~ and the rest) without the browser ever seeing a held Ctrl or Alt. ~Escape~ turns it on (see the priority order above), or on a phone the *[g]* button does ([[#god-mode-mobile][below]]). While it is on, every key is part of a sequence instead of a plain shortcut, and the minibuffer (see [[#modeline][Modeline and minibuffer]]) echoes the sequence.

God-mode starts on the heading you last used, or else on the row at the top of the screen. Running a block with ~C-c C-c~ keeps the cursor on it.

When a sequence completes, the minibuffer names what ran, using the command palette's own label: ~God-mode · C-c C-x C-j → Go to clocked task~. A chord with no palette command (~Tab~, the arrows, ~C-f~) shows just the chord. The name stays until the next keystroke. Entering god-mode focuses the first visible heading if none is focused, since its actions need one.

While a sequence is in progress, a card under the top bar lists the keys that would continue it and what each does, as Emacs's which-key does. Each entry is a button: tap it to send that key, so a whole chord can be completed by tapping, with no device keyboard. A key that leads on to more is marked ~…~. ~Escape~ cancels the sequence and the card goes away.

Opening an overlay panel (the Extras menu, Settings, Docs, Capture, Search, the File, View and More menus, the History panel or the Calendar) exits god-mode, and the plain shortcuts don't act while a panel is open; ~Escape~ closes the open panel first. Help opened with ~h SPC m~ is the exception (see below).

The translation rules follow real god-mode.el (github.com/emacsorphanage/god-mode), plus the ~c~ rule, which is this app's own:

- A plain key means Control: ~t~ is ~C-t~.
- ~g~ prefixes the next key with Meta (~g↑~ is ~M-↑~), so a bare ~C-g~ can't be typed. ~G~ (Shift+g) prefixes Control+Meta (~Gn~ is ~C-M-n~).
- ~SPC~ toggles literal mode: following keys are typed with no modifier until ~SPC~ is pressed again. ~c SPC g~ is ~C-c g~, not ~C-c C-g~.
- A named key (arrow, Tab, Return) typed bare is never controlled, so ordinary movement keeps working.
- ~c~ as the first key gives ~C-c~ and starts an org-style chain: further letters are controlled too (~c t~ is ~C-c C-t~, ~c c~ is ~C-c C-c~) while punctuation stays literal (~C-c .~, ~C-c |~). One ~c~ is enough for any ~C-c C-<letter>~ command.

| god-mode sequence | Emacs chord | Action |
|---+---+---|
| ~↓~, ~↑~ | ~<down>~, ~<up>~ | Next or previous visible line; inside a table, the next or previous row |
| ~←~, ~→~ | ~<left>~, ~<right>~ | Collapse or expand the heading; inside a table, the previous or next column |
| ~S-↓~, ~S-↑~, ~S-←~, ~S-→~ (the floating *S* then an arrow, or Shift+arrow) | ~S-<down>~, ~S-<up>~, ~S-<left>~, ~S-<right>~ | On a focused heading: move it down or up among its siblings, promote it (left) or demote it (right), like the heading's action buttons. In a table they move between cells. With nothing focused, ~S-↓~ and ~S-↑~ go to the next or previous heading. On a laptop, ~Alt~+arrow moves, promotes and demotes the heading from anywhere, even in a table |
| ~S-←~, ~S-→~ | ~S-<left>~, ~S-<right>~ | Table cell to the left or right |
| ~i~ | (not a chord) | Edit the current line, cursor at the start (see ~a~ and ~e~) |
| ~a~ | ~C-a~ | Before ~i~: put the cursor at the start of the line |
| ~e~ | ~C-e~ | Before ~i~: put the cursor at the end of the line |
| ~Tab~ | ~Tab~ | Cycle the focused heading's fold state |
| ~S-Tab~ | ~S-Tab~ | Cycle the whole document (overview, fully shown) |
| ~←~, ~→~ | ~<left>~, ~<right>~ | Collapse the focused heading fully, or expand it one level |
| ~g↑~, ~g↓~ | ~M-↑~, ~M-↓~ | Move the focused heading up or down among its siblings |
| ~g←~, ~g→~ | ~M-←~, ~M-→~ | Promote or demote the focused heading with its subtree |
| ~gS-←~, ~gS-→~ | ~M-S-←~, ~M-S-→~ | The same (there is no separate whole-subtree action) |
| ~c f~, ~c b~ | ~C-c C-f~, ~C-c C-b~ | Focus the next or previous heading at the same level; a status message says when there is none |
| ~c u~ | ~C-c C-u~ | Focus the parent heading (a status message at the top level) |
| ~c n~, ~c p~ | ~C-c C-n~, ~C-c C-p~ | Focus the next or previous visible heading, at any level |
| ~c SPC l~ | ~C-c l~ | Copy an ~[[id:…]]~ link to the focused heading (~org-store-link~) |
| ~c x w~ | ~C-c C-x C-w~ | Cut the focused heading and its subtree to the clipboard (~org-cut-subtree~) |
| ~c x y~ | ~C-c C-x C-y~ | Paste a subtree after the focused heading at its level, shifting the pasted levels to match (~org-paste-subtree~) |
| ~x SPC n s~ | ~C-x n s~ | [[#narrowing][Narrow]] to the focused heading's subtree |
| ~x SPC n w~ | ~C-x n w~ | [[#narrowing][Widen]]: remove any narrowing |
| ~x SPC x r~ | ~C-x x r~ | *Rename buffer…* (~rename-buffer~): ask for a new name in the minibuffer. An empty name or one another buffer has is refused; the file is not touched |
| ~gRET~ | ~M-RET~ | Insert a heading after the focused one, as its sibling. With nothing focused, an empty document gets a heading at the top and a document with headings gets one at the bottom |
| ~gS-RET~ | ~M-S-RET~ | The same, with a TODO keyword |
| ~c t~ | ~C-c C-t~ | Cycle the focused heading's TODO state; with no state and more than one ~#+TODO:~ workflow, open a state picker |
| ~c ,~ | ~C-c ,~ | Cycle priority (none, A, B, C) |
| ~c v~ | ~C-c C-v~ | Switch to the TODO view |
| ~c .~, ~c !~, ~c d~, ~c s~ | ~C-c .~, ~C-c !~, ~C-c C-d~, ~C-c C-s~ | Open the details editor (SCHEDULED, DEADLINE, timestamps) |
| ~c w~ | ~C-c C-w~ | Refile the focused heading (~org-refile~, see [[#refile][Refile]]) |
| ~c a~ | ~C-c C-a~ | Open the attachment choices (~org-attach~, see [[#attachments][Attachments]]) |
| ~c SPC a~ | ~C-c a~ | Open the Agenda view |
| ~c SPC c~ | ~C-c c~ | Open Capture, which exits god-mode (see below) |
| ~h SPC m~ | ~C-h m~ | Open Help (~describe-mode~) without exiting god-mode |
| ~s~ | ~C-s~ | Open search |
| ~x q~ | ~C-x C-q~ | Toggle ~buffer-read-only~ (see [[#local-variables][Local Variables]]) |
| ~x s~ | ~C-x C-s~ | Save (~save-buffer~) |
| ~x SPC s~ | ~C-x s~ | Offer to save every modified tab that has a file, one key each (~save-some-buffers~) |
| ~x w~ | ~C-x C-w~ | Save under a new name or place (~write-file~, Save As) |
| ~x f~ | ~C-x C-f~ | Open a file (~find-file~) |
| ~c x SPC e~ | ~C-c C-x e~ | Set the focused heading's effort estimate (~org-set-effort~, see [[#clocking][Clocking]]) |
| ~c x i~ | ~C-c C-x C-i~ | Clock in (~org-clock-in~) |
| ~c x o~ | ~C-c C-x C-o~ | Clock out (~org-clock-out~) |
| ~c x q~ | ~C-c C-x C-q~ | Cancel the running clock without recording its time (~org-clock-cancel~) |
| ~c x x~ | ~C-c C-x C-x~ | Resume the most recently clocked heading (~org-clock-in-last~) |
| ~c x j~ | ~C-c C-x C-j~ | Jump to the clocked-in heading, in whichever tab it runs (~org-clock-goto~) |
| ~u c x j~ | ~C-u C-c C-x C-j~ | Choose from recently clocked tasks and jump to it (~org-clock-select-task~) |
| ~c e~ | ~C-c C-e~ | Open the export dispatcher (~org-export-dispatch~, see [[#export][Export]]) |
| ~f~ | ~C-f~ | Arm the next ~/~ to redo instead of undo |
| ~/~ | ~C-/~ | Undo, or redo if armed |
| ~g x~ | ~M-x~ | Open the [[#command-palette][command palette]] |
| ~h SPC a~ | ~C-h a~ | The same (~apropos-command~: find the commands that match) |

Some valid sequences have no equivalent yet and say so instead of doing nothing: ~c c~ (toggling a checkbox or running a code block needs finer focus than a heading), ~c |~ and the table row and column inserts (use the +row and +col controls under any table), and ~c l~ and ~c o~ (there is no link insertion or cursor-based link opening).

*Pickers*: ~c SPC c~, and ~c t~ on a heading with no TODO state and several workflows, exit god-mode and show a picker. Its options are tappable buttons, each also labelled with a one-character hotkey you can type at once. A hotkey is shown and accepted only when no other option shares it; those options are tap-only. Opened any other way (a tap, the ⋮ Capture button, a TODO-less heading's badge), the pickers show no hotkeys. ~Escape~ cancels either.

*Help*: ~h SPC m~ doesn't exit god-mode. While Help is the only thing open, god-mode keeps working underneath it, and ~Escape~ cancels a sequence and then exits god-mode instead of closing Help. Opening any other panel, or leaving god-mode, restores the ordinary rule.

*Redo*: Emacs has no redo command; it undoes the undo, after something breaks the chain (god-mode users conventionally press ~C-f~). Here ~f~ just arms the next ~/~ to redo. ~/~ keeps redoing while armed, any other key disarms it, and with nothing left to redo ~/~ falls back to undo. The palette's *Undo* and *Redo* are unaffected.

*~i~, ~a~ and ~e~* aren't chords; they are loosely modeled on vim and act only as the first key of a fresh sequence (~g i~ is still ~M-i~ and ~c i~ still ~C-c C-i~). ~a~ and ~e~ set where the cursor lands the next time ~i~ opens the editor, and say so in the minibuffer (~C-a → edit at start (press i)~). Once editing, every key is ordinary text-field input.

-----

*** God-mode without a hardware keyboard
:PROPERTIES:
:CUSTOM_ID: god-mode-mobile
:END:

A phone has no ~Escape~ key, so a floating *[g]* button, the third floating button, stacked above Extras or in its place when there is no Extras menu, does three things together: it enters god-mode, shows a floating keyboard and brings up the device's keyboard. Tapping it again ends all three, and it is drawn solid while the keyboard is showing. It rides above the mode line and the device keyboard, and nothing already on screen moves for it. Settings → Quick Settings → *Keyboard* has a *Show the floating [g] god-mode button* checkbox (~org-xx-god-mode-button~, on by default) for devices with a real ~Escape~ key. A document's Local Variables line overrides it, and turning it off while the keyboard is showing ends god-mode.

The floating keyboard has the keys a phone keyboard can't type, in one row: *⌨*, ~Tab~, ~←~, ~→~, ~↑~, ~↓~, ~S~ and ~g~. Its thick accent-coloured border makes it easy to spot, and the keys are 34px wide and 44px tall so the row fits a 360px screen.

- *S* shifts the next key (~Tab~ becomes ~S-Tab~, ~g~ becomes ~G~, the Control+Meta prefix). After an arrow it stays on, so ~S~ then ~↑~ ~↑~ ~↑~ moves the focused heading up three places; tap *S* again to turn it off. It also shifts the next key typed on the phone keyboard, so ~gS-RET~ (~M-S-RET~, a TODO heading) is: tap ~g~, tap *S*, tap Return. A letter typed after *S* becomes its capital.
- *⌨* hides or shows the device keyboard and changes nothing else. It is lit while the keyboard is up. After a popup closes, the keyboard doesn't return by itself; tap ⌨.
- The move area (⠿) drags the panel, and its position is remembered. Tap it without dragging to minimize the panel to its handle, and tap the handle to restore it.

*Placement*: the panel sits above the mode line and the floating buttons, so the device keyboard never hides it and it never covers the mode line or *[g]*. By default it sits just above the floating buttons. If the keyboard comes up under it, it is pushed up and stays there when the keyboard goes away; only dragging lowers it.

*Lifetime*: god-mode and the panel end through *[g]*, ~Escape~ or another panel opening, never because the device keyboard went away. Hide the keyboard however you like and god-mode, the panel and its keys carry on, leaving the whole screen to read the outline. Entering god-mode with a real ~Escape~ never shows the panel.

If a letter doesn't register on your keyboard app, the command palette reaches the same commands by name.


** Differences from Emacs org-mode
:PROPERTIES:
:CUSTOM_ID: differences-from-emacs-org-mode
:END:

For readers who know Emacs org-mode: where org-pwa does less or differs. A topic not listed here behaves as in org.

*Interaction model* (see [[#keybindings][Keybindings]]): touch-first, not keyboard-driven. The [[#command-palette][command palette]] is ~M-x~ only in spirit: a fixed, curated list that you can't add to, not every Emacs command. god-mode's table doesn't cover table cells, per-list-item checkboxes or link insertion (see [[#god-mode][god-mode]]).

*Folding* (see [[#editing-your-outline][Editing your outline]]): no equivalent of Emacs's richer visibility state machine, but three flags per heading, on top of which ~overview~, ~content~, ~showall~, ~showeverything~ and ~show2levels~ to ~show5levels~ are implemented.

*Priority, tags, properties* (see [[#editing-your-outline][Editing your outline]]): tags and property keys complete from what is used in the open document and loaded agenda files (tags also from a ~#+TAGS:~ line). Priority is a fixed A/B/C/None row with nothing to complete, and nothing is treated specially beyond ~CUSTOM_ID~ and the ~ARCHIVE_*~ set.

*Inheritance* (see [[#local-variables][Local Variables]]): property inheritance is a simple boolean. Tag inheritance takes ~t~, ~nil~, a list or a regexp, and ~org-tags-exclude-from-inheritance~. Both apply to search, to the Agenda and TODO tag filters, and to the dimmed inherited tags shown after a heading's own tags (switched by ~org-xx-show-inherited-tags~ in the outline and ~org-agenda-show-inherited-tags~ in the Agenda).

*Tables* (see [[#table-formulas][Table formulas]]): ~#+TBLFM:~ covers arithmetic, conditionals, named constants, scalar and aggregate functions, date and time arithmetic and formatting, and unit conversion. Complex numbers and basic vectors and matrices are covered; not reproduced: the rest of Emacs Calc (symbolic algebra), named-field references, and recalculation on every keystroke.

*Footnotes* (see [[#footnotes][Footnote commands]]): in the outline a footnote goes in through the Footnote button of the paragraph editor, and there is no ~org-ref~ integration.

*Clocking* (see [[#clocking][Clocking]]): no custom ~org-duration-units~, no ~Effort_ALL+~, and no clock-in reminder beyond the modeline's over-estimate marker.

*Agenda* (see [[#agenda][Agenda]]): only the effort keys of ~org-agenda-sorting-strategy~ are read. ~org-agenda-prefix-format~ knows ~%c~, ~%t~, ~%s~ and ~%e~. The sexp evaluator is a Lisp subset without ~setq~ or function definitions, and ~org-class~ skips only US and Christian holidays. A ~local:~ agenda file is read-only.

*Babel*: ~js~ blocks run, with ~:results~, ~:var~, ~:timeout~, ~:wrap~, ~:net~, ~:location~, ~:cache~, ~:noweb~ and tangling (see [[#source-blocks][Source blocks]] and [[#literate-programming][Literate programming]]). These do not exist: blocks in any other language, ~:session~, running one block from inside another (~<<name()>>~), and results that refresh when a file is opened.

*Links and structure*: ~[[id:...]]~ links are followed through the open tabs and Agenda Files, then the files opened here before, from a table kept in this browser rather than ~org-id-locations~. ~<<targets>>~ and radio targets work in the outline and in every export. ~#+SETUPFILE:~ is read from the same place as the document, or from an http(s) URL, and kept for offline use. *Citations* (see [[#citations][Citations]]): LaTeX export honours ~natbib~ and ~biblatex~; every other export uses the ~basic~ processor, so ~csl~ is exported as ~basic~. ~note~ styles print as ~text~, and ~org-cite-export-processors~ is not a setting (use ~#+CITE_EXPORT:~).

*Undo/redo* (see [[#undoredo-and-history][Undo/redo and History]]): no undo tree, and fold state isn't preserved across an undo or redo jump (the file's ~#+STARTUP~ visibility is reapplied). There is no per-keystroke granularity; the browser's field-level undo covers that, much as Emacs batches consecutive typing.

*Search* (see [[#searching][Searching]]): Search and Replace both reach every file in ~org-agenda-files~, as org's ~org-search-view~ and ~tags-query-replace~ do. Both subtree narrowing (see [[#narrowing][Narrowing]]) and Search's Narrow survive a reload.

*Export* (see [[#export][Export]]): ODT, As-org, Calendar (.ics) and Contacts (.vcf) are palette commands; the Export menu lists ASCII, HTML, LaTeX and Markdown. LaTeX follows ~ox-latex~ from Org 9.6 (Emacs 29.3 bundles 9.6.15) and was checked against Emacs on about 40 samples, including this README. It offers only the ~article~, ~report~ and ~book~ classes (no Beamer, no ~org-latex-classes~), writes source blocks as ~verbatim~ (no ~minted~ or ~listings~), leaves ~\author~ empty without ~#+AUTHOR:~, and names the app in ~pdfcreator~. Newer Org versions differ in small details such as blank lines. ASCII export matches ~ox-ascii~ for characters, entities, blocks and lists, but lays out headings, tables and links its own way (numbered headings with indented bodies, tables with ~|~ borders, links as ~description (target)~, no ~Notes~ list of links). Justify-left and justify-right blocks are set as ordinary text, which is what Emacs 29.3 produces too. HTML export differs from ~ox-html~ in a few deliberate ways: its own colouring instead of ~htmlize~, KaTeX instead of MathJax, readable element ids, real checkboxes, ~::~ inside code or verbatim text is not a description-list separator, and no ~#+HTML_DOCTYPE:~.

*Refile* (see [[#refile][Refile]]): you can't create a new destination heading by typing a name that doesn't exist yet.

*Attachments* (see [[#attachments][Attachments]]): the same folder model as ~org-attach~ (an ~ID~ or ~DIR~ folder and the ~:ATTACH:~ tag) and the dispatcher keys ~a~ ~b~ ~n~ ~o~ ~f~ ~d~ ~D~ ~s~ ~S~ ~z~, plus ~r~ to record audio. The Folder panel stands in for ~org-attach-dired~: select files, then open, save or delete them. Not built: copy, move and link (~c~, ~m~, ~l~), attaching from a Dired buffer, and ~DIR~ paths outside the storage. Needs GitHub, WebDAV, or the org-pwa folder in the Android app.

*Conflict resolution* (see [[#offline-behavior-and-sync][Offline behavior and sync]]): a line-based three-way merge with a region-by-region resolver. It merges lines, not org structure, so a subtree moved on one side and edited on the other is an ordinary clash, and a region has no side-by-side or word-level diff.

-----

** Known limitations / not built yet
:PROPERTIES:
:CUSTOM_ID: known-limitations--not-built-yet
:END:

Gaps against org-mode itself are in [[#differences-from-emacs-org-mode][Differences from Emacs org-mode]]. This section covers app-specific and platform limits:

- Local and relative images show a placeholder on local files (File System Access) and iOS imports, the same picker-permission limit as archiving and capture to a file. GitHub and WebDAV documents are unaffected.
- No File System Access on iOS, a platform limit rather than a bug (see [[#platform-support][Platform support]]).
- A read-only buffer accepts no edit anywhere in the document, though Save and Save As still work, as in Emacs (see [[#keybindings][Keybindings]]).

-----

** Development
:PROPERTIES:
:CUSTOM_ID: development
:END:

A static site: ~index.html~ and ES modules, with no build step to run or deploy it. Serve it any way you like, including ~python3 -m http.server~ or GitHub Pages.

The one exception is ~src/vendor/mathjs/mathjs-custom.min.js~, a tree-shaken custom mathjs build (Unit, BigNumber and Fraction, used by [[#table-formulas][Table formulas]]'s ~uconv()~, ~F~ and ~pN~). It is regenerated occasionally with ~tools/build-mathjs-vendor.sh~, a dev-only step; the committed output is what ships, as with the vendored KaTeX files.

*Tests*: the engine (~src/~) and the browser adapters (~src-browser/~) use Node's built-in test runner, with no external dependencies:

#+BEGIN_SRC
npm test
#+END_SRC

The tests run with a frozen clock, so they give the same result on any day. ~npm run test:zones~ runs them in five time zones.

Behaviour that Emacs defines is held to Emacs itself. ~tools/gen-repeat-oracle.mjs~ and ~tools/gen-agenda-oracle.mjs~ ask Emacs 29.3 (with ~faketime~) what completing a repeating task does and which days the agenda lists; ~tools/gen-latex-oracle.mjs~ does the same for LaTeX export, and ~tools/latex-compile-check.mjs~ compiles the output. The answers are stored the answers under ~test/fixtures/~; the tests compare the app with them.

~npm run lint~ (ESLint) and ~npm run typecheck~ (~tsc~ on files that begin with ~// @ts-check~) need ~npm install --no-save eslint @eslint/js globals typescript~. ~node tools/release.mjs N~ checks, bumps the cache name and writes ~org-pwa-vN.zip~; ~.github/workflows/ci.yml~ runs the same checks and the smoke test on every push.

~node tools/roundtrip-corpus.mjs DIR~ checks that every ~.org~ file in a directory comes back byte for byte after an open and save with no edit.

One test checks that every module the app imports is in the service worker's precache list, because nothing is cached at runtime and a missing module would stop the app starting offline.

*Code layout*: ~app.js~ is the entry point (about 1,400 lines): it imports everything, sets up the shared state, wires event listeners and runs ~bootstrap~. Features live in ~src-browser/~, one module per area. All runtime state is one object, ~S~, in ~app-state.js~, and the page's DOM elements are looked up once in ~dom.js~. The split is by file rather than decoupled (modules call each other, so the import graph has cycles), and browser modules need a DOM, so Node can't import them. ~test/module-structure.test.js~ and ~tools/check-scope.mjs~, a scope analysis that needs the acorn and eslint-scope parsers installed once (~npm install --prefix /tmp/acorn acorn eslint-scope~), keep the structure from decaying.

Everything the app asks of the device (files on the device, saving a file out, the clipboard, the service worker) goes through ~src-browser/platform.js~, which has browser defaults. A native shell supplies its own by setting ~window.orgPwaPlatform~ before the app loads, and hands a share to ~window.orgPwaLaunch()~. The browser tests use a fake platform the same way.

*Browser smoke test*: it covers what unit tests can't reach, since ~app.js~ is UI wiring:

#+BEGIN_SRC
node tools/smoke.mjs             # everything
node tools/smoke.mjs conflict    # only checks whose name contains "conflict"
SMOKE_SLICE=0:27 node tools/smoke.mjs    # only the first 27 checks; 27: runs the rest
#+END_SRC

It drives the real app in headless Chromium through flows that have broken before, against a built-in static server and a small in-memory WebDAV server. It is dev-only, adds nothing to ~package.json~, needs Playwright and a Chromium once (~npm install -g playwright && npx playwright install chromium~, or set ~CHROMIUM_PATH~), and exits non-zero on any failure.

~test/testing.org~ holds an older record of the testing approach and is no longer maintained.
